Monti Carlo’s Caribbean Cowboy Caviar

Andrea Rivera WawrzynFood Editor
Andrea Rivera WawrzynFood Editor
I've worked in the food industry for 15 years as a chef, recipe developer, writer, and editor. Prior to joining the Kitchn team I was an associate editor at America’s Test Kitchen, a contributor to Serious Eats, and worked on cookbooks for Ten Speed Press, Rebel Girls, and Clarkson Potter!

I’ve been cooking for a very long time. I was taught how to navigate the kitchen, and what went with what, when I was a youngster by my Latin American family. As a kid who lived in New York City, though, my tastes extended beyond the scope of Latin and Caribbean flavors to the American fare I was growing up around. I loved cheese omelettes and chicken nuggets just as much as I loved pastelitos, pernil, and sofrito-laced beans. 

The marrying of these two perspectives is what attracted me to Monti Carlo’s new cookbook, Spanglish, in which she masterfully blends familiar-to-me Puerto Rican flavors with just-as-familiar American ones. I was thrilled to get the chance to chat with her about how she thinks about blending cuisines and telling her story in her first cookbook. 

This book isn’t quite a memoir, but it does take the reader on a journey through your story. Not all cookbooks are so forthcoming with the details of the chef’s life. What made you want to share so much of yourself in your first cookbook?

Spanglish isn’t just the title of the book or the style I adopted for the recipes. It’s an identity. It’s my identity. I was raised between Puerto Rico and the continental United States, constantly moving between two places that were both home. Like a lot of kids who grow up between cultures, I never felt like I was enough of either one. The essays explain how I found my sense of belonging in the space between.

I also wanted to keep it real. I don’t have this perfectly polished life, and I have zero desire to present one; I just can’t live up to that. For me, it’s far more powerful to show the moments that almost broke me, because that’s where real growth happens. Those moments shaped me much more than my successes did. That’s why I don’t get caught up in debates about whether something is “Puerto Rican enough.” If someone tells me my beans aren’t Puerto Rican because I put olives in them, I shrug it off.

Food is a language, and language evolves. Language changes as people move and adapt to new places, as culture evolves. Cuisine works the same way. Every generation shapes the recipes it inherits. For me, food became the thread that connected every version of home. Spanglish is really about giving yourself permission to exist (and cook) between cultures without feeling like you have to choose one over the other.

I come from a bicultural Puerto Rican family as well, and I love seeing the creative mix of Puerto Rican cuisine with American dishes. How do you think about blending those flavors? Where do you start?

Honestly, I started with the grocery store. I’ve always hated the idea of the “ethnic” aisle. It low-key tells us which foods “belong” and which don’t. But Latinos make up about one in five Americans, and Puerto Ricans have been U.S. citizens for more than a century. We’re not going anywhere. 

Not everyone gets to visit Puerto Rico, but almost everyone goes to the grocery store. To me, that’s where food becomes familiar. If our ingredients are shelved alongside everyone else’s instead of tucked away in a separate aisle, maybe people stop seeing Puerto Rican food, and Puerto Ricans themselves, as something “other.” Maybe then it’s a little easier to understand that we’re not foreigners. We’re your neighbors, your coworkers, your classmates. We’re Americans with a distinct culture, history, and cuisine.

Food has always been one of the easiest ways to understand another person, and sometimes all it takes is seeing a bottle of adobo next to the Italian seasoning to realize we have more in common than we think. That’s also why I don’t ask someone who’s never cooked with a plantain to start by making mofongo. That’s a big leap. But would they make crispy chicken nuggets coated in crushed plantain chips? Absolutely. Would they stir passion fruit juice into a curd the same way they’d use lemon juice? I bet they would. That’s really the philosophy behind Spanglish. I’m not trying to make Puerto Rican food less Puerto Rican. I’m trying to make Puerto Rican ingredients feel like they belong in every American kitchen. Because if Puerto Rican food becomes part of people’s everyday lives, maybe it becomes a little easier to remember that Puerto Ricans are American, too.

I know it can be hard for a cookbook author to pick a “favorite” recipe from the book, but is there a recipe (or recipes) that’s a staple in your kitchen?

The guanábana pound cake is my favorite recipe in the book because it isn’t really about the cake; it’s about my abuela. She ate a slice of Sara Lee pound cake almost every day. The aluminum loaf pan it came in, with the crimped edges, was nearly impossible for her to open because of her arthritis. I was about 4 years old, and it was my job to pry the lid off. Those aluminum edges hurt like hell, but opening that container made me feel like such a grown-up. Then I’d slice her a piece with a butter knife while she made herself a cafecito. When she was eating her pound cake and having that coffee, I wasn’t allowed to talk. It was her one moment of peace.

I created the guanábana pound cake recipe for her. We had a guanábana tree growing up, and I couldn’t help but imagine what would happen if I folded that flavor into the cake she loved so much. My abuela has been gone for more than 30 years now. I wish I could bake that cake for her just once. I wish I’d known then how little time we had left together. When you’re a kid, you assume there will always be another cup of coffee, another slice of pound cake, another afternoon at the kitchen table. Every time I make that cake, for just a moment, I get to sit back at that table with her again.

If someone has never had Puerto Rican food before, what’s your recommendation for a good recipe to start with?

I’d start with the Salsa Criolla Shakshuka. Salsa criolla is one of the foundational sauces of Puerto Rican cooking. It’s one of those recipes that teaches you so much about our flavor profile: sweet peppers, onions, garlic, tomatoes, and herbs.

Turning salsa criolla into shakshuka makes it approachable. Most people are familiar with shakshuka. (In case you’re not, it’s a one-pan dish of eggs simmered in a vibrant tomato sauce with Middle Eastern and North African origins.) Introducing salsa criolla into the recipe should feel like you’re making this familiar comfort food through a Puerto Rican lens. That’s what Spanglish is all about. It’s also one of those recipes that checks every box. It’s budget-friendly, easy enough for a weeknight, beautiful enough for brunch with friends, and delicious any time of day. Set it on the table with some crusty bread to soak up all that super-flavorful salsa criolla. Oof —that’s my kind of meal.

Caribbean Cowboy Caviar Recipe

A Caribbean twist on the classic bean salad with mangoes, sweet peppers, and dressing with a touch of spice.

Prep time 20 minutes

Makes 10 1/2 cups

Serves 6

Nutritional Info

  • shellfish-free
  • gluten-free
  • vegetarian
  • pork-free
  • red-meat-free
  • high-fiber
  • soy-free
  • pescatarian
  • dairy-free
  • alcohol-free
  • fish-free
  • peanut-free
  • egg-free
  • tree-nut-free
  • wheat-free
Per serving, based on 6 servings. (% daily value)
  • Calories 428
  • Fat 11.5 g (14.8%)
  • Saturated 1.9 g (8.1%)
  • Carbs 69.7 g (23.8%)
  • Fiber 16.4 g (43.1%)
  • Sugars 21.6 g
  • Protein 16.3 g (13.9%)
  • Sodium 984.3 mg (65.6%)

Ingredients

Dressing:

  • 3 tablespoons

    olive oil

  • 1

    Finely grated zest and juice of 1 lime

  • 1 tablespoon

    Pique (recipe below)

  • 1 teaspoon

    adobo seasoning

  • 1/2 teaspoon

    kosher salt

  • 1/2 teaspoon

    light brown sugar

Salad:

  • 1 (15-ounce) can

    garbanzo beans

  • 1 (15-ounce) can

    pink beans

  • 1 (15-ounce) can

    black beans

  • 6-7 ounces

    sweet peppers (red, orange, yellow), seeded, and cut into a small dice

  • 3

    Roma tomatoes, hulled, and cut into a small dice

  • 2

    honey mangoes (also called Ataulfo mangoes), peeled, seeded, and cut into a small dice

  • 1/2

    medium red onion, cut into a small dice (1/2 cup)

  • 1 (packed) cup

    chopped fresh cilantro

  • Kosher salt

  • Plantain chips, for serving

Instructions

Make the dressing:

  1. In a liquid measuring cup, whisk together the olive oil, 2 tablespoons of lime juice, lime zest, the Pique, adobo, salt, and brown sugar, until the sugar has dissolved.

Make the salad:

  1. Line a baking sheet with paper towels. In a colander set in the sink, combine the garbanzo, pink, and black beans. Rinse them well with cool water and drain, then pour them onto the prepared baking sheet and pat dry.

  2. In a large bowl, combine the beans, sweet peppers, tomatoes, mangoes, red onion, and cilantro. Pour the dressing around the inside of the bowl and mix gently so the vegetables are evenly coated.

  3. Cover and refrigerate until well chilled. Stir and add salt to taste before serving with plantain chips.

Comments

Pique Recipe

Prep time 5 seconds

Makes 2 cups

Nutritional Info

  • shellfish-free
  • tree-nut-free
  • soy-free
  • pescatarian
  • no-oil-added
  • gluten-free
  • vegan
  • egg-free
  • vegetarian
  • peanut-free
  • dairy-free
  • wheat-free
  • low-fat
  • pork-free
  • red-meat-free
  • alcohol-free
  • fish-free
Per serving, based on 2 servings. (% daily value)
  • Calories 165
  • Fat 1.0 g (1.3%)
  • Saturated 0.2 g (0.8%)
  • Carbs 30.4 g (10.4%)
  • Fiber 4.5 g (11.9%)
  • Sugars 16.6 g
  • Protein 4.2 g (3.6%)
  • Sodium 958.9 mg (63.9%)

Ingredients

  • 1 1/2 cups

    distilled white vinegar

  • 1/2 cup

    pineapple juice, preferably fresh

  • 1 teaspoon

    granulated sugar

  • 1 tablespoon

    kosher salt

  • 6

    serrano peppers, stemmed and cut in half lengthwise

  • 4

    red bird’s-eye (Thai) chile peppers, stemmed and cut in half lengthwise

  • 2

    Scotch bonnet chile peppers, stemmed and cut in half from top to bottom (may substitute habañeros)

  • 1 (1x4-inch) strip

    of lime zest (no pith)

  • 6 cloves

    garlic, peeled and smashed

  • Small knob of fresh turmeric, smashed

  • 5

    whole black peppercorns

Instructions

  1. In a clean 1-quart, wide mouthed jar, combine the vinegar, pineapple juice, sugar, and salt, stirring until the sugar and salt have dissolved.

  2. Add the serrano, bird’seye, and Scotch bonnet peppers, the lime zest, garlic, turmeric, and peppercorns, stirring to distribute them evenly. Make sure the peppers are completely submerged.

  3. Seal and let stand at room temperature in a sunny spot from 3 days to 3 weeks to allow the flavor to develop. Afterward, refrigerate (to keep it from intensifying further) for up to 1 month.

Recipe Notes

Contrary to popular belief, Puerto Ricans don’t use many hot peppers in their cooking. Instead, our favorite flavor is agridulce, or savory-sweet. But, of course, there are always exceptions to the rule, and that’s where pique comes in. You’ll find this vinegar-based hot sauce on most Boricua tables; everyone has their own version. It’s used in the same way you would use any hot sauce, to add a little fire to savory preparations. Traditionally, pique is made with ají caballero, a tiny hot pepper that grows abundantly on the island. But most grocery stores on the big continent don’t carry this beauty, so Spanglish-it-up and substitute it with your favorite hot pepper. You can leave the peppers whole, but I prefer to cut them in half lengthwise to give the vinegar access to all those extra-hot seeds!

For optimal results, let your pique ferment in a sunny spot for at least a few days. If you need some right away, add the vinegar, pineapple juice, sugar, and salt to a small pot and bring them to a simmer. Then, take it off the heat and add the rest of the ingredients, giving them a quick pickle.

Sometimes, garlic turns a blueish green in vinegar. Don’t be alarmed; it’s just enzymes having a chemical reaction to the acidity. Blue garlic is still perfectly edible. The color of the serranos might dull a bit in the vinegar, but the bird’s-eye and Scotch bonnet peppers will remain vibrant. As you go through the pique, don’t hesitate to refill the bottle with more vinegar and peppers. It’s okay to add them to the old batch! Pique is vinegar-based and can last indefinitely in the fridge, though I keep mine at room temperature.
